utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We had a bit of a late start which was caused by the request for the witness to do some homework. And he could finish it if he would have a tiny little bit more time, which was granted. Mr. Kovacevic, first of all, it is appreciated that you have done the homework you were asked to do. Thank you for that. I further would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that is, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Jordash, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to go through the transcript from the previous case in which you testified? Did you have enough time this morning?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reviewed the transcript. It was a bit hard, but I managed to get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to make notes and make any corrections, if any corrections were needed, to what you'd said at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made some notes, and I made some corrections as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Should we go through those corrections now? Would you like to go through them one by one and indicate what it was you read and what it was you noticed that you would like to correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, let's go through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I inquire, how much -- how many corrections, approximately, will we have to deal with? Are there five, are there 20, are there 70, or are there just 3? Could you give us an indication.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only a few. Maybe two or three corrections for the sake of clarifying certain facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can proceed the way you suggest, Mr. Jordash. I take it that you are aware that you have to link them in one way or another the time because the witness watched the video, the time with the transcript pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll do what I can, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could invite the witness that, if he makes any correction, that he uses one or two specific words he found in that portion of the transcript so that we are better able to identify where to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have on e-court, please, 1D01212.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And while that's happening, we're talking, are we not, Mr. Kovacevic, about a time you testified on the 12th of May, 2009? Is that right? When you testified previously, it was on the 12th of May, 2009, at this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was in May of 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, would you indicate, please, what your first correction is. And in order to assist us finding the place in the transcript, please read out the sentence or sentences you would like to correct.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first correction refers to the transport of men to the Republic of Serbian Krajina. There is inconsistency in the statement and in the transcript. In the statement that I gave, it was written that two buses had left for Knin in a -- or, rather, Republika Srpska; whereas in cross-examination, there's mention of three buses, which is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So in -- when you were asked questions by the Prosecution, you stated that two buses had left for Knin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe we are at 6079 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we could go to that on e-court. 6079. I'm not sure I can see it on 6079.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First line, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh, I see what's happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you referring, Mr. Kovacevic, to the suggestion by the Prosecution from the question: "When you arrived at the barracks, you indicated that there were three buses at your disposal. How many buses in total were there?" Your answer was: "There were six or seven buses in all." Is that the section of the transcript that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the section of the transcript that I'm referring to. In my statement, I said that two buses were sent to the Republic of Serbian Krajina; however, during cross-examination, it is recorded in the transcript that three buses left for Republika Srpska, which is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you would say your answer -- your evidence is now that two buses left for the Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbian Krajina; more precisely, Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right, okay. That's your first correction. And your second?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second correction -- but let me first say that it should have been recorded that there were one or two TAM 190 JNA buses and three or four buses owned by private hauliers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. That's what -- something you would like --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were also two vehicles of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, i.e., three buses; two of them went for Knin and one went to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Is that what you wanted to add to that section of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And second, what would you wish to correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it reads in the transcript that on the way back from Knin to the Republic of Serbia there were 20 or 25 officers and non-commissioned officers who had served there, and there is mention of Major Vladimir Tomasevic. Mr. Tomasevic left with me to Knin, but he stayed in the Army of Republika Srpska. He didn't come back to Belgrade with me. In one segment of the transcript, it is said that he returned to Belgrade alongside me, which is incorrect. However, this was clarified in cross-examination with Defence counsel Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the correct version is that you gave in cross-examination? There's no need to add anything to the transcript; is that what you're confirming?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, just to be clear, we don't need to add anything to the transcript; your evidence is that which was given in cross-examination. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If I can take you, then, to your next correction, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next correction is as follows: In March of 1994, in Borovica Transport Company for the needs of MUP, I took a lorry tanker 1735 with a capacity between 25 and 26 tonnes of liquid.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you referring to a section of the transcript when you're seeking to add this evidence? If so, what is the sentence or paragraph you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't see this particular sentence on my monitor. This correction refers to the period in 1994 when we took the vehicles from Borovica Transport to be used by the MUP of Serbia, and I would just like to say in this context that Mercedes 1735 was taken to be used by MUP of Serbia, and I said its capacity was some 25 or 26 tonnes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. I think we're dealing with page 6058 of the transcript, so if we could have that on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, are you referring to this statement of yours --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Line 15, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "The first job of work, the first trip of fuel took place, if I'm not mistaken, in the month of March 1994. I received orders from my superior to report to the Borovica Transport Company." Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you want to add that the Mercedes 1735 was taken to be used by the MUP of Serbia, and its capacity was some 25 or 26 tonnes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the licence -- the licence plate of that truck was a Ruma 22501, and the trailer had licence plate number 1526 Ruma.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we go to page 6060, I think we have reference there to -- at line 9: "It was Mercedes 1735, the make, and the fuel tank had the capacity of some 26 to 27.000 litres." Am I correct, Mr. Kovacevic, you'd like to add what you've just told us, about the Mercedes and its capacity, to that piece of evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I added the licence plate numbers for that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any other corrections?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Apart from those corrections, if you were asked the same questions again, you would give the same answers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably. It's been a long time ago. I'm not sure I can repeat it verbatim. There must be some differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But the substance would be the same? The expression might be slightly difference, but the substance would be the same?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I apply, please, for this to be admitted pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D96 -- I apologise, D97, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D97 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, I want to return to the subject we were dealing with yesterday and your notes. Where were they kept?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been keeping the notes at home. The last I had them with me was when I came to The Hague in August of last year, however, nobody asked to see them. I put them back where they used to be. I explained to my wife last night their whereabouts, however she didn't manage to find them. She only found my statements, both in Serbian and in English, that I gave to the Tribunal. She spent the time until 2.00 in the morning but couldn't find the notes. But I would like to say that I undertake here that I will find them and I will furnish them to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Where did you put them in your house? Where were they put for safekeeping?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kept them in a cupboard next to the kitchen elements on the wall next to the fridge. My wife doesn't know exactly how these documents look like, although I tried to explain to her last night; but, nevertheless, she couldn't find them. And obviously I'll have to do it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, how big is the cupboard?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately 2.6 metres in height, 80 centimetres in depth, and 1.4 metres in width.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we have -- I asked to go back into open session. You wanted to address me, Mr. Kovacevic. We are now in open session. So if you would raise any matter which you'd prefer to raise in private session, we'd first have to return into private session. I don't know what you wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need for us to go back into private session. As the Defence counsel has suspicions about me possibly forging these notes, that would be impossible because these were dispatch receipts. And besides, all the documentation connected with trucks exists in the seat of the Centrex company and in the treasury of the Republika Srpska agency in Bijeljina with Mr. Ranko Sukalo. The documentation can be consulted there, and Their Honours can see for themselves the quantities and the goods involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There's another matter, Mr. Jordash. You most likely are aware that with forensic techniques it should not be that difficult to make a distinction between documents that were, if that would be the case, produced a week ago or ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we agree on that, I take it. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But, Mr. Kovacevic, you've now limited your description of your notes to dispatch receipts and documents connected with trucks within -- within the seat of the Centrix company and within the treasury of the Republika Srpska agency in Bijeljina. So are you now saying you don't have notes of the people you met; it is actually just a collection of receipts -- dispatch receipts that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was mentioning these documents on the issue on convoys. However, in short, these notes contain notes of the 1st of October, 1991, made in Eastern Srem at the front line there where I started writing them in the village of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which village did you start writing them in?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Vera, which is located just across the bridge at Bogojevo from Serbia into Croatia. You have Erdut and then Principovac farm estate. And next you have the village of Vera. From there, you could take the dirt road to Pacetina, Brsadin, and other villages. Specifically, the then-president of the Serbian Radical Party for the Republic of Croatia Rade Leskovac hailed from the village of Vera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And your notes go, then, from 1991 until when?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kept the notes from 1991 up until 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on from the notes, shall we.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I have, please, on e-court page 2167 of the transcript in this case. Okay, I don't think we need it on e-court, but that's what I'm going to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Kovacevic, we dealt with the meetings that you'd had with Mr. Stanisic, and you gave us an account. Having reflected overnight, I imagine, do you have anything further to add about meeting Mr. Stanisic at any other place?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I no longer met Mr. Jovica Stanisic. I was thinking about -- well, I didn't have time, actually, to think about other matters related to him since I was occupied with the business surrounding the notes and the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. You didn't meet, did you, Mr. Stanisic in any other place than, according to you, Belgrade and when you were a security detail during the -- let's call it the hostage crisis?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I saw Mr. Stanisic when I was accompanying my superior who went with him to his office in the seat of the state security department. The second time was at the Danube port. And the third time was with the hostage crisis. And the fourth time was at the celebration where awards were granted to special police units at Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. You never saw him in Erdut at any time, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw Mr. Jovica Stanisic at Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, when you gave evidence a year ago in this court, on oath, you claimed that you'd seen him in Erdut in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 2167.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And yet you have a very clear recollection today of not seeing him in Erdut. What's the truth?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, as I was driving my superiors to the meeting at Erdut, I was told that Jovica Stanisic was there as well. However, when I got back home from my testimony, I went through my notes and realised that this was not true. And once my notes are delivered to the Prosecution, this will become quite apparent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, when you gave evidence in August of 2009 in this court, you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 2166.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "I saw him, Mr. Stanisic, for the first time in the centre of Erdut. I drove my superior to a meeting in Erdut to see Mr. Badzo." Later on you said, when asked, Was Mr. Stanisic on his own, line 9 of page 2167, you answer: "I think there were other -- three or four people accompanying him." So you gave very clear evidence about a very clear recollection of Mr. Stanisic being with three or four other people. It follows, doesn't it, that you invented that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is what I was told. At the meeting in Erdut in 1991 of the members of the state security department that I personally saw and knew, there was Mr. Stojic who was posted to the state security department in Kragujevac --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the language on page 2167, line -- well, the first four lines is non-unambiguous.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, but the language on page 2166, "I saw him for the first time in the centre of Erdut" is, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now -- I've forgotten whether the witness understands any English. Mr. Kovacevic, do you understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take off your earphones for a second. Mr. Jordash, the possible ambiguity on 2167, if you accept that as ambiguity - and I said it's non-unambiguous, so I'm very cautiously phrasing it - could have an effect on the whole passage. That's -- I'll not further go into any details, although I could, but then we would have the witness ... but do you understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's clear to you, then let's proceed. Could you put on your earphones again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's be clear, Mr. Kovacevic, did you ever see Mr. Stanisic in Erdut in 1991, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you ever told that he was present, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In which circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that Mr. Jovica Stanisic came to the training centre in Erdut. I myself didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: To the training centre for what?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the training centre of the Serbian Volunteer Guard of the Arkan's Tigers. Subsequently, it was also the training centre for the milicija, the police of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What were you told about his presence there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was said that he came to the meeting of the command cadre that was present in the area in command of the units. I wasn't specifically told any further details how and why and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of my superiors told me so, Mr. Veljko Miletic, who attended several meetings in Erdut, Dalj, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was Miletic doing telling you that? What was the circumstances which led to him telling you that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Veljko Miletic was, up until 1991, deputy commander of the police station in Pakrac in the Republic of Croatia, and when for the first time rebellion was organised there, he was the one leading ethnic Serb policemen. Subsequently, he left that post and came to work in the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What were you doing with him when you had the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I became good pals with him at the time when we were members of the reserve force and before we were deployed to the front line. This because the difference in age between our respective sons was one year. And then subsequently when he came to Belgrade I assisted him in finding a flat and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, the question simply was: "What were you doing with him when you had the conversation?" You are telling us the whole of the background of your relationship with him. The only thing Mr. Jordash wants to know is what were you doing with him; were you in a bar, were you at -- in the Erdut camp? What were you doing when he told you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was assigned to be a driver of my superior in my unit and otherwise was a member of the platoon, the commander of which was Mr. Veljko Miletic. Since we were billeted to the various houses in the village of Vera, we were billeted to the same room.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So he told you this prior to Mr. Stanisic arriving, or after Mr. Stanisic had come and gone some days later? When?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly when he told me this, whether it was at a time when Mr. Stanisic was there or whether this was several days earlier. I was sent to the village of Brsadin, I was assigned there, and it would so happen that I wouldn't see my commander for several days in a row.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So he told you it in the village of Vera, did he, where you were billeted?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Our unit was stationed some -- was stationed in the village of Vera for some 35 to 40 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Miletic tell you that Stanisic had visited, and did that conversation take place in the village of Vera where you were billeted?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To the best of my knowledge, Mr. Stanisic never came to the village of Vera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you phrase your questions more directly, more short and sharply, then we might get the information you apparently are seeking, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you have the conversation with Miletic in the location where you were billeted in Vera?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we discussed many things both having to do with our job and with our private lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So that's a yes. Let's see what you said when you gave evidence in this case a year ago. "I drove --"

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 2167:

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "I drove my superior to a meeting in Erdut to see Mr. Badzo. I was standing next to my car together with Captain Zeljko Sucic when a vehicle came by. Some people came out and Captain Sucic told me that Jovica Stanisic had arrived." So no mention last year about this conversation with Miletic; is there a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it wasn't "Vukic." Rather, it was Captain Zeljko "Sucic."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, thanks for the correction. Is there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, Mr. Jordash seeks the following to be clarified: Last year, in this courtroom, you said: "I drove my superior to Erdut ... I was standing next to my car together with Captain Sucic when a vehicle came by. Some people came out" - I take it, out of the vehicle - "and Captain Sucic told me that Jovica Stanisic has arrived." That's your testimony of last year. Now, today you tell us that the visit of Mr. Stanisic to the Erdut camp, that you heard about that in a conversation you had with Miletic in the village of Vera. These are two different stories. What Mr. Jordash want to know is whether you -- which one, if any, is the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Captain Zeljko Sucic told me, at the time, that Mr. Jovica Stanisic had arrived. And then he went on to attend the meeting. Then, as he came out of the meeting and returned to our camp, Mr. Zeljko told me that he was mistaken, that Mr. Jovica Stanisic had not been present there at the time. Now, I learned later on from Mr. Veljko Miletic, who regularly attended meetings at Erdut and Dalj, that Jovica Stanisic had been present, though I myself did not see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, why didn't you tell us last year that that was a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't say that. I probably forgot. I was asked if he was there and then I said, Well, yes, I was in Erdut. But I didn't go into details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I did -- I do not consider it a detail that if you tell us that Mr. Sucic told you that Mr. Stanisic had arrived - I do not consider it a detail if you leave out that he later told you that Mr. Stanisic had not been there and that he had not arrived. That's not a detail. That is totally the opposite of what you told us. Any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that point, this was the statement I made. Then as I returned to Belgrade and looked into my notes - and I had made notes on a daily basis - I realised that this piece of information was untrue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you immediately contacted whom to inform us that you made a very heavy mistake when giving your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't contact anyone upon my return home. As I was coming out of this courtroom and going home, I was told not to contact anyone and not to tell anyone about what had transpired in the courtroom since I was still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, then you came back to this Tribunal to continue to be examined. Why didn't you - the first thing you told us - that I want to correct a heavy mistake I made last year: I went through my notes, and I gave you the wrong information. Why didn't you tell us immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know I was supposed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kovacevic, why didn't you then, having checked your notes, think about bringing your notes with you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I took the notes with me to the ICTY field office in Belgrade in February of 2003. They cast a glance at them and asked me to copy two maps out of them. For the rest, they told me that I should keep them. Now, just before I was about to make this trip, I forgot to take the notes along because I had undergone a surgery and I was out on Monday and on Wednesday I arrived in The Hague. So on Monday I was out of the hospital and already on Wednesday I was on my way to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on then. Am I correct that you did not in April of 1991 go to Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in April of 1991. I didn't go to Borovo Selo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And am I correct that you do not know who was present there, which militarised groups were present?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the first time I heard of the events in Borovo Selo was from TV on the 1st of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you have no idea whether or who from the DB -- let me start that again. Do you know if the DB had anything to do with Borovo Selo in April of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we have on e-court, please, P51. And I'm looking, please, for paragraph 16. And can we go over the page on the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You see the paragraph? Please read it, Mr. Kovacevic, and read particularly the last -- sorry, the second to last sentence: "In April of 1991, Serbian volunteers from Serbia were sent to Borovo Selo. They were members of the Serbian Radical Party and the Serbian National Renewal, and men from the DB of Serbia were also present there." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It follows, doesn't it, Mr. Kovacevic, from your last answer that you don't have information about the DB in Borovo Selo in April of 1991, that this statement is not correct? Doesn't that follow?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This paragraph 16, at the time when I gave this statement, contains some facts that I had heard either on TV of Serbia at the time or from some friends of mine who had come from that area. In addition to that, since I was living at the time in Surcin, there were as far as I know five or six volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party who had gone to that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You have no idea whether the DB were in Borovo Selo and yet you signed a statement saying they were. Could you explain why you did that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that the DB was in Borovo Selo. I said that men were on the ground in Eastern Srem. I did not say specifically Borovo Selo. I mentioned that all this was organised in the Serb populated areas. I made no specific mention of Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we could take the statement off the screen for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please explain your role, if any, in transporting weapons from Serbia to a ferry on the Danube in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My role was that of a driver during the period that started in mid-June 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And how many times did you do it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. Three or four times perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who ordered you to do it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was ordered by my superior officers at the police brigade because we had 4, 12, 13 Mercedes trucks and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the other type of trucks and their number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please repeat the second type of trucks and their number, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were FAP 1620 trucks. I think there were two or three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. I don't think we needed the detail about the trucks, so can you try to limit your answer to the question. Who was your superior who ordered you to do this assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received this order from my company commander, Mr. Plavsic. And during the loading and transportation, I was accompanied by an active-duty policemen whom we used to call Paja. He was, at the time, also a storekeeper for the brigade, and he was the one who issued and received back all the items that we had with us. Actually, he was the warehouse manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And this transport of weapons -- sorry, this -- yes, this transport of weapons over the Danube involving Paja, what role did Paja play?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paja would issue items and goods and he would go with us to accompany the goods and see to it that it was handed over on the left bank of the Danube whilst it was being loaded on the bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What did this have to do with the DB?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that on one occasion somewhere near Novi Sad at one petrol station we were met with some people in plain clothes. Mr. Paja and Mr. Milan Ilic, who was also a truck driver and he was an active-duty police officer who came from Sibenik in Croatia, said that we have been now taken over and escorted by the DB.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So this conversation you had with Paja and Milan Ilic were in your truck, were they? Were they in your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Paja was with me, and Mr. Ilic was driving behind me, so when Paja went to see those men who were in civilian clothes and he came back while Milan and I stood by his truck. And that is when he told us that we had been taken over by the people from the DB who would escort us to the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And those people from the DB were in their own vehicle when Mr. Paja told you this?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Paja came back to the trucks, these four men went into the car and they went to the head of the convoy and we set off.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So Paja and Mr. Ilic and the four men had spoken in a vehicle behind your vehicle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that Mr. Paja and Mr. Ilic talked to those men. I said when we stopped at the petrol station that Paja approached this vehicle, while Ilic and I were standing next to our truck. Paja talked to these men for a short period of time, then he came back and these four men got into their car and went to head the convoy. I didn't say that they talked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you hear anything that was said to the DB men or by the DB men?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear this conversation that took place between them and Paja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And during that particular assignment, you -- well, did the DB men ever speak again to Mr. Paja or Mr. Ilic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When we reached the bank where the ferry was supposed to come, some men were awaiting us there. The goods were offloaded, and we went back because we were drivers. And Paja stayed with those men and returned to Belgrade with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you never got a chance to confirm, yourself, by speaking to them personally, who they were; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never talked to them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And they never talked to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They just said at one point that we opened the tarpaulin and the back sides of the trucks and to have the trucks ready for offloading as soon as possible because we couldn't stay there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that was said from the DB men to who? Who did they say that to?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To all of us. They said, Lads, please hurry up, open the trucks for them to be offloaded quickly so that we can remove ourselves as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That was the only thing you heard them say; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I complied with that. Those who were waiting there, climbed onto the trucks. Everything was done very quickly. Everything was offloaded. And then we went back to our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we have P51 on e-court, please. Paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. Jordash. Could we have this off the screen. Mr. Kovacevic, I carefully listened to your answers. Did I understand you well that it was exclusively because Paja had told you that the DB was now taking over that you knew that these four men were of the DB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was because Paja told you, not because they had told you; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't say anything to anyone else. While we were at this parking-lot near the petrol station, their car was already there. And as an officer at the time, because he had a rank, I don't remember which particular rank --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment. Later, when there was offloading, at that time these people just said hurry up and did not inform you that they were DB people; is that correctly understood as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They just said to carry out the offloading as quickly as possible without mentioning at all to which service they belonged or anything else. They were just going from one truck to another and checking up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. May I take it that you want the witness to read paragraph 18?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't want to have him read it yet. There are some other things I'd like to go through first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. At the same time, I'm looking at the clock. We have approximately 75 minutes spent until now, therefore perhaps it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break, and we'll resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are a few matters which require our attention before we continue. The first one is the next witness. Mr. Jordash, perhaps the cross-examination develops a bit different from what you would have expected, I do not know, but has this any impact on timing?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Ideally, I would like the rest of the day. Ideally. I'm about a third to 50 per cent of the way into the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see the point. I also would urge you to try to speed up under the circumstances as you deem fit to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes certain matters appear to have been clarified already quite a bit or being confused perhaps at such a level that it may not always make sense in every -- on every subject to continue to explore that situation any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, the Chamber would really urge you to finish your cross-examination today. Mr. Groome, that means that the next witness, it's of no use to have him on standby. Would you need a lot of time in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I expect no more than three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, VWS can be informed about the next witness in accordance with what we just discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll see to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there's another matter that is about next week. The Chamber is at this moment exploring the possibilities of sitting also on Wednesday afternoon despite your negative expectations as what we could achieve, Mr. Jordash, in terms of finishing testimony of witnesses next week. The Chamber, nevertheless, wants to keep that option open and never gives up the hope that we become very efficient and get the evidence to us as quickly and as succinctly as possible without losing anything. So, therefore, Wednesday afternoon, certainly not the whole of the afternoon but at least part of it, is a option the Chamber wants to keep point open and is further exploring as to its feasibility. Having said all this, Mr. Jordash, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, we were discussing the involvement of the DB in the transportation of weapons. Am I correct, from what you said before the break, this was the only occasion that you were involved in when you saw the DB also involved?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on that occasion, but it may have happened again once or twice. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is the only occasion, then, that you remember the details; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And from what you've said, you were coming from somewhere around Novi Sad, you drove the DB -- the four DB men joined the convoy, and then you arrived at the Danube; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The weapons were then offloaded; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You -- were you involved in the offloading?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We helped for it to be offloaded as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Paja was the logistics man, is that right, with a ...

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paja was a logistics man because he was responsible for the brigade depot, police brigade depot. After the offloading was completed, he stayed with these other men to oversee the further dispatch of the goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And so the only stop that was made on this journey was when the four DB men joined the convoy and led the convoy to the Danube; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was at a NIS petrol station on the Belgrade-Subotica road, and the petrol station is called Minuta.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And there was no other DB men involved in this convoy other than the four you've told us about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to P51 on e-court. Paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Paragraph 18. I want to try to move as swiftly as possible, Mr. Kovacevic, so if you would try to keep your answers short. Please read paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "He told me to report to the 1st Company to a man called Paja from the depot. The both of us went to fill the tanks with diesels, and then we went to Bubanj Potok barracks, which is near Belgrade. I parked there and remained in the truck."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, you were only invited to read for yourself. That's what you had in mind, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please read for yourself paragraph 18 and then Mr. Jordash will put the questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just take a slightly different approach now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now that the witness has read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you've just read that sentence, is this the occasion we're talking about when you met the four DB men?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The four DB men were waiting for us at the Minuta petrol station, whereas during the unloading in Bubanj Potok, the soldiers who were there told us that there were also men from DB present who were overseeing the loading process.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Just listen to the question, please. The description you've just read in paragraph 18 is the same occasion that you've been telling the Court about; am I correct, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only the four men who waited to us near Novi Sad were not present during the loading in Bubanj Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Because you do say at paragraph 18: "Four men in civilian clothes came up to me and introduced themselves, saying they were from the DB. They said from that moment on I was to obey their orders only." That's not correct then, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct because during the loading in Bubanj Potok and when we came down there, they told our leader Paja, the man from the logistics, that we were to obey their orders from then on and to load whatever they say should be loaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, I'm trying to have you pay attention to the detail of what it says. And it says that the four men came up to you and introduced themselves to you saying they were from the DB, which is different to the account you gave before the break. Which account is correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that when we came to VP 1960 Bubanj Potok, Paja was with me in a car. When we got out, four men in civilian clothes approached us, as well as some soldiers -- actually they approached Paja, but I heard them saying that those were their colleagues from the DB and that we were to obey their orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. If that's your answer, let's move on. Paragraph 19: "One of those men sat with me in the driver's cab and showed me how to get to the depot, where I parked the truck again and opened its trailer." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true he sat with Paja and me in the cab. Since we were at the head of the column, we went to the depot where the soldiers who were supposed to load the trucks were waiting for us. And the loading was being, as I said, overseen by these men and Paja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you did have a conversation with the men from the -- with one of the men from the DB? Before the break you said you hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't talk to the men who were waiting for us at the Nis petrol station, but as for those who were present while the loading was in progress, I talked to them for a while. Paja got out of the cab, he shook hands with them, and he said that we were to obey their order.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraph 20: "We loaded crates with weapons and ammunition. When this was done, we left. A jeep with civilian plates and two DB operatives in civilian clothes went ahead of my truck. There was also a Yugoslav-made Zastava 101 civilian vehicle behind my truck. The vehicle had civilian Belgrade number plates, and two DB plain-clothes operatives were in it." Did you tell the Prosecution that there were two more DB plain-clothes operatives in addition to the four that you've told us about in paragraph 18?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two operatives joined us when we set off from Bubanj Potok towards Novi Sad. They followed us in a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So there's now six, according to your account in the statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because two of them continued to drive in a car after us, but at Mostarska Petlja intersection, the one who was with me in the cab left; whereas the others followed us until we reached Novi Sad and then went back. And at that point the other four were taken -- were the ones who took us over and escorted us to the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Picking up on paragraph 20: "We picked up another DB operative at the Mostarska Petlja intersection." So, are you -- at that -- sorry, let me start that again. Did you tell the Prosecution in 2003 that there was a seventh DB operative present during this convoy?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The seventh operative replaced his colleague who got out of my cab. Paja was sitting in the middle, he was sitting next to the door, and he alighted at the Mostarska Petlja intersection, and another colleague of his took his place. He was in the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Did any of these seven DB operatives show you their DB state security identification card?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm correct, aren't I, that during your time between 1991 and 1996, let's say, you saw a number of DB operatives who showed you their state security identification card, the same one that you told us about yesterday, that Arkan possessed; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They showed it to me on a number of occasions. I specifically remember Zoran, an operative who was from somewhere near Pozarevac, he told me that he was a DB operative. Also on the front line where I went later, Mr. Stojic, who was another DB operative assigned to the DB section in Kragujevac, and Mr. Dragan Miletic, aka Zuca.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. And they all had the same card that Arkan had; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was similar or not, I can't say because they didn't show me the cover. They just opened it and told me, We are members of the DB. I even continued to socialise with Mr. Miletic, aka Zuca.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And each of those cards that you saw had state security -- the words "state security" written on them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that, and I didn't pay much attention, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So it was only Arkan's card which had "state security" on it, the other that is you saw did not?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not "state security" that was written; it was only written "security service."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. So each of these cards that you saw belonging to DB operatives and Arkan had "security service" written on them; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the only cover that I saw was the ID that Arkan had. The others only opened their IDs and told me that they were members of the DB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, in order to avoid further confusion, if you ask questions about what is on the identity cards, could you always make the distinction between the cover and the inside --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because otherwise we get even more confusion than we have already. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Arkan's identification, according to you, had "security service" written on the outside, on the cover; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was blue in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you see that card with "security service" on the cover in the possession of anybody else during 1991 to 1996?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it in anybody else's possession. I can tell you that I saw the ID at a distance of some 3 to 4 metres because he was, in fact, showing his ID to my superior as they were discussing a conflict that I described. I can't even claim for a fact that it contained his photograph, since I saw it from a distance of 3 to 4 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just going back to the subject of this convoy, before the break you said there was only four DB operatives, now having looked at your statement from 2003 you say there were seven. Was there four or was there seven?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the petrol station, since this is what we discussed before the break, near the place called Novi Sad, there were four operatives waiting for us, and they escorted us onwards. Whereas the individuals who escorted us up to Novi Sad returned to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. If that's your answer, let's move on. This, just to be clear, was in 1991, towards the end of 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not towards the end of 1991, it was sometime in the summer of 1991, before the death of the command of Borovo Selo defence, Vukasin Soskocanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you say that you were working in the reserve forces of the JNA or the reserve forces of the MUP of Serbia at this point?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point, I was transferred to the reserve force of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And at what point do you say you were working or you were transferred to the reserve force of the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once I deliver my military booklet, you will see that I was transferred in April of 1991. I was listed with the Zemun municipality, the Office for National Defence there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat the address that he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What is the address that you just mentioned, Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Surcinski Put bb at Bezanijska Kosa, where the anti-sabotage unit and the unit for training and use of dogs is -- was present. And the latter unit was part of the police force. Since the HQ of the police was on Trebevicka Street, in the event of a state of war, the assembly point was to be at Surcinski Put.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you for the information. Where is your military booklet?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My military booklet is still kept by Jovanovic, Zivorad, the clerk who was in charge of my reserve unit within the MUP. It's still with him because I never picked it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we have on e-court, please, 1D01212.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is, Mr. Kovacevic, your testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think it's D97, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, when D97 was admitted into evidence, you may have overlooked that parts of it are confidential. And that's the reason why I instructed Madam Registrar to have it under seal for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would you please keep this in mind. So that means that if we put it on the screen that -- without having verified which portions are and which portions are not under seal, that certainly it should not be shown to the public. And when reading and referring to it, you're also invited to carefully consider possible confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 6053 of that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Line 14, you were asked this question: "I'd like to highlight specifically, how were you employed in 1994 and 1995?" Your answer: "In 1994, in -- or, rather, in earlier January 1992, or in the month of December, I was transferred from the reserve forces of the JNA to the reserve forces of the MUP of Serbia; to be specific, to the police brigade of the MUP of Serbia." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in April of 1991 that I was transferred, and this can clearly be seen in my military booklet. I attended a two-month course at the School for the Internal Affairs at Zemun.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, in the Perisic trial, that's not what you said. Was that a slip-up? Because is the truth that you actually were not in the reserve forces of the MUP until much later and you've invented a story to implicate the accused?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not invent this in order to implicate the accused. It was in late August that I went to Zemun as a member of the reserve force of the MUP with my unit and my platoon. I even named the members of my platoon in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, can you name some of them then, please? Who were you -- who was in your unit in 1991? And we know who you say the commanders were, but who was in the unit with you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to avoid -- the witness said "platoon," I think he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then specifically ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- for names of those who were with him in his platoon. Have you heard the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just -- I'd like, if I may, to ask him about who was in his police brigade in 1991. The witness says he was in the police brigade in 1991 belonging to the reserve force of the MUP, and it's that information that I'd like to seek, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Please proceed. I just want to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was assigned to the 3rd Battalion, 1st Company, 1st Platoon, unless I'm mistaken. The commander of my battalion was Mr. Milosevic. Company commander was Mr. Plavsic. And the platoon commander -- my platoon commander was Mr. Steva Pavkovic. Then there was Zoran Miletic, Pera Ojkic, Milan Ilic, Zaric, and other individuals whom I can't recall at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How many people in the brigade unit in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 35 men in my platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you were with them from 1991 on several occasions until, am I correct, 1998, or later than that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was with them at the front line. Later on, I was posted to Kosa 3, which was located on the motorway to Zagreb near the Sivanovci exit point. The leader of that point was Mr. Bakovic, as well as Bogdan from the traffic police unit on Ljermontova, and Zoran Mutavcic was my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Going back to 1991, you've named, I think, five names out of 30. Can you name any more who you were with in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can name, as far as I remember, Mr. Milan Markovic as a member of my unit. Then there was Dejan Mitic, a native of Leskovac. And there were other individuals. I can't remember all of their names now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: These were all police officers, were they?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were all policeman. Mr. Veljko Miletic had come from the SUP of Pakrac. Mr. Ilic had come from the SUP of Sibenik. Mr. Stanko Kukic had come from the MUP of Croatia, from Zagreb, as well as Mr. Steva Pavkovic. From among the policeman were born in Serbia, there was Milan Markovic, Dejan Mitic, and others. Mr. Zoran Mutavcic hailed from Pakrac; he used to work in the Croatian MUP in Pakrac and then moved to Serbia. Whereas Mr. Zaric was from Bjelovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know where any of these people are now, the ones you've just named? Where they live?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am in touch with them. Mr. Zjelko Miletic holds the rank of lieutenant and works in the Sid Police Station. For awhile he was deputy commander of traffic police, whereas now he is the commander of border police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Markovic works for the Zemun Police Station. Mr. Pero Ojkic works for the traffic police unit at Ljermontova Street, and he attends scene-of-traffic accidents. Mr. Ilic, to my knowledge, remained a member of the police brigade. Then an individual --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- works for the traffic police. Zaric is retired. Stanko Kukic passed away. Whereas Spiro Arcabas, who had come over from the Zadar SUP, was killed in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. There was one person, Mr. Ojkic, who you said worked for the traffic police unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He still works for the SUP in the traffic police department, and he carries out on-site investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's on Ljermontova Street. And the seat is in the current SUP on Savski Venac. They are assigned to different quarters of town. You have police stations north, south, and east.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you explain, please, how it was that you, a reserve member of the MUP, was allocated the job of driving -- driving Mr. Sljukic [sic]? Why were you chosen as a reserve member of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a decision made by my superiors out in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But it's, am I correct, unusual to the point of being unique for such a job to be given to a reserve member of the MUP? The driver for a commander is always - I submit to you - a full-time member, someone who can be verified and trusted; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I was not out at the field at the front line, I drove Mr. Slobodan Vukolic, deputy commander, although I was not a part of the active force. Mr. Vukolic now has the rank of colonel and is head of the administration of the city of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, your previous question was a rather composite question which contained a lot of details. Don't be surprised, also on the basis of your experience you have until now, that you get the kind of answers you would think would not assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In 1991, having, as you say, joined the reserve force of the MUP of Serbia, was your principal job to drive Slobodan Vukolic, deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Slobodan Vukolic was not deputy commander. At that point, he was assistant commander of the brigade. I drove him whenever I was assigned to the police brigade. When I was not there, there was another member of the reserve force from Zemun who was his driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you were called for duty in 1991 as a member of the reserve force of the MUP, was your principal job, your main job, driving Slobodan Vukolic, the assistant commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Initially he didn't have that position. It was from Eastern Slavonia, from that front line that I would drive him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. And Eastern -- he was in Eastern Slavonia when?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in late August up until the liberation of Vukovar. Vukovar was liberated on the 18th of November, and we stayed in the field up until the 25th or 26th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So from late August until November was your principal job driving Slobodan Vukolic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was your principal job?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My job in the field was to be the driver for the staff unit. I had a schedule, and I would drive people to the observation post at Brsadin silos, which was just next to the place called Brsadin and just on the edge of Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can add: I was also charged with driving senior officers according to the schedule that I would be given at the HQ. I would take them either to the meetings at Dalj or to the battalion that was stationed in the village of Vera, where we were billeted, or to other meetings as required.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Another subject, Mr. Kovacevic. Would you agree with me that you have no evidence to suggest that the Serbian state security were responsible for forming and controlling all the paramilitary units from 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the forming of the Serbian Volunteer Guard and the subsequent arrival at the frontline of the unit called Knindze which were trained down there near Knin - perhaps at Golubic, I'm not sure - at any rate, there was a unit that came from down there in September. According to the information I had, those units had been trained by Captain Dragan. At the time, we only knew him as Captain Dragan. We later learned that his name was Dragan Vasiljkovic who had been engaged by the state security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So apart from Captain Dragan's Unit and the Serbian Volunteer Guard, you have no evidence and cannot confirm that the DB was responsible for any other paramilitary group; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the DB, well, I can't claim that they were responsible for a paramilitary group at that point in time in the field, but they were responsible for the Serbian Volunteer Guard because members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard were much better armed than we were and the JNA units that were present in that area. We had old flak jackets that weighed 27 kilos; their's weighed 4 kilos. They had modern weaponry; we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that in a minute. Let's just stick to my question, if we can. Apart from the Serbian Volunteer Guard and the unit trained by Captain Dragan, do you have any evidence that the DB was responsible for any other paramilitary unit? Yes or no will do, I think.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't claim either way. The only thing I know is that when Radovan Stojicic, Badza, was appointed commander of the Territorial Defence in that area, there were stories to the effect that he was directly subordinated to the state security service. To what extent that is true, I cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, Mr. Kovacevic, I'm not sure that the issue of Badza -- well, okay, let's forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please could we have on the screen P53.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to refer you, Mr. Kovacevic, to something that you appear to have said the 24th and 25th of August, 2009. Paragraph 2 states: "From 1991, the state security pulled the strings. All paramilitary units were formed by the Serbian state security and were under its control." And you signed that document, didn't you, Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you accept that that was, to put it kindly, an exaggeration?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not an exaggeration. The Territorial Defence of Western Srem -- or rather, the Territorial Defence of Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem was under the control of Radovan Stojicic, Badza, that's to say of the state security. Members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard were also under the control of the DB, as were the Knindze Units that arrived in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, let's deal with that. Let's go --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I add that commanders of the defence of the villages were chosen by members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard and members of the Territorial Defence under the command of Radovan Stojicic, Badza. On what basis they chose individuals who were to be commanders of defences of villages, I don't know. I knew commander Brsadin and Mr. Savo Milosevic as commanders of defence of the various villages because I was there in contact with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Kovacevic, could I ask you the following: At one point in time during the last five minutes, you say that there were stories to the effect that Badza was directly subordinated to the state security service, and you added to that: "... to what extent that's true, I cannot tell." Now, three minutes later, you say: "The Territorial Defence of Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem was under the control of Radovan Stojicic, Badza, that's to say of the state security." So at one moment you say there were rumours, I do not know whether they are true; and then three minutes later you say Badza, that is, the state security. Are you still referring to the rumours or do you have any specific source of knowledge why you now say Badza, that is, state security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, specifically speaking, I personally heard from Mr. Savo Milosevic, commander of the Brsadin defence, that he was appointed by Radovan Stojicic, Badza, himself. A lot of meetings were held between our commanding officers and Mr. Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and some 70 or 80 per cent of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. There are two elements in this question: The first is whether Badza was chosen -- whether he was commanding the defences of the villages, that's downwards, who were the men under him. And the other question is a totally different question, whether Badza was directly subordinated to the state security. Your answer is about the lower level; my question was about Badza as an element of the state security where you first say these were rumours, I do not know whether they are true, and where you now say, Badza, that is, state security.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was receiving orders from Radovan Stojicic, Badza. Even my units and my commanding officers would receive some orders from Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and were reporting back to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I quickly take instructions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's have a look what you -- your account was in 2003, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please could we have on e-court P51.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We are going to have a look, Mr. Kovacevic, about what you said then about the role of the Serbian MUP and the DB.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Paragraph 38, please. Sorry, paragraph 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you see that? Just have a read of it to yourself, please. Have you read that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you accept that's -- do you say that's true, that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In early August 1991, we arrived in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, specifically to Eastern Slavonia and West Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You didn't, in 2003 when giving the Prosecution that answer, say that Arkan was under the control of the DB, did you, which would seem to be a significant piece of information?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say then that Zeljko Raznjatovic was under that control. What I said was that we arrived at this SUP of Croatia centre in Erdut and that it was being used by Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan's Units.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just so that I understand so I'm clear, your evidence is that the state security was in control of Stojicic, Stojicic was in control of Arkan; was that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, is it; because the bridge at Bogojevo, which was the only crossing point between Serbia and Croatia, was controlled by units of Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. Which means that units of the Yugoslav People's Army were not deployed at this bridge. The flow of people and goods was controlled by the units of Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Are you suggesting that your unit was also under the control of Stojicic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
