utterances.text: As member of the MUP of Serbia, my unit received orders from the TO of Western Srem and Mr. Radovan Stojicic, Badza; and we also cooperated with JNA units deployed at the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you were -- and your unit was supplied by -- sorry, let me start that again. Your unit received weapons and ammunition from the MUP of Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We came dressed in blue camouflage uniforms and with blue berets on our heads, and we brought rifles and service pistols with us. We also had ammunition with us, and later on the ammunition was replenished, either by the JNA or the TO. But, anyway, our depot manager or depot keeper was in charge of those supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to paragraph 37 on the screen, if we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the paragraph 37, the last line, says: "The JNA was far better armed than we were." Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the JNA units were better armed than our MUP units of the Republic of Serbia because they had heavy weapons, mortars, artillery, multiple rocket-launchers, tanks, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: They had more sophisticated weaponry than those supplied to the MUP forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had automatic rifles and pistols, 7.62 millimetres, and, if necessary, we carried with us to the field Zolja rocket-launchers and hand-grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go to paragraph 41, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There you make comment about, in the second sentence, about: "Radovan Stojicic, Badza, commanding our unit. We received orders for combat action from the JNA, but Radovan Stojicic, Badza, had to be informed of these orders and approve them before we were allowed to act upon them." No mention there, Mr. Witness, about Badza receiving orders from the DB.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A meeting was held every evening, attended by JNA officers, as well, deployed in the area, and agreements were reached between Mr. Radovan Stojicic, Badza, commanders of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, the territorial units deployed there, and our units.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yet no mention about the DB being in command. Isn't it correct that the first time you mention that was in 2009 when you came here to testify in this case and you were spoken to by Mr. Hoffmann?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Radovan Stojicic, Badza, co-ordinated actions with the Serbian Volunteer Guard as well as with our units and JNA units. As for the engagement of units of the Serbian Volunteer Guards and the rest of it, as far as I heard from my officers he received orders from the state security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When did you remember that information? Why didn't it go into your 2003 statement, but you only seem to have remembered it in 2009?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because when I was giving my statement in 2003, the investigators who came to Belgrade didn't go into any details. First of all, when I gave this statement in 2003 in Belgrade, my statement was taken without any knowledge in which case it was going to be used. I was informed only in 2006 or 2007 about the possibility of me giving evidence against Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that's when you remembered how they had been in control of Badza; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I remembered. When I arrived in The Hague and the Prosecutor raised this question during proofing and I explained it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And for Your Honours' information, that's at paragraph 6 of the proofing note, P53. I've just been reminded of the time, Your Honour, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we resumed at a quarter past 4.00 and we have now 75 minutes. We'll have a break. But perhaps we first ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom. We'll have a break of approximately half an hour, Mr. Kovacevic. Could we escort -- could you escot Mr. Kovacevic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, two brief issues: The first, yesterday you were very eager to achieve that the notes would be obtained before the witness would return home again. That seems to be at this moment not very practicable. I do not know whether -- to what extent you still want to go after the notes. He has offered that he will bring them, but he also said that he would first return to his home and then bring them. Is that -- is the urgency -- I mean, I hardly see any possibility to get this all done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I think the witness -- it's impossible to obtain the notes, it seems, before the witness returns home. If we obtain the notes, then we'll make what submissions we can at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see -- we'll then see what happens. Okay. We leave is it to that. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to ask the Chamber to give specific instructions with respect to the notes. And I'm happy to do that now since we are talking about it, or I can wait until before he is excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Instructions to be given to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would the instructions be you had on your mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would first ask that the Chamber instruct VWS to give the witness a large, sealable envelope addressed to this Chamber noting the name of this case as well as Mr. Kovacevic's name. I would ask the Court to instruct Mr. Kovacevic to do the following: That he place his notes in that envelope and seal the envelope, that he be explicitly instructed not to review the notes or to make any corrections of any kind to the notes or any additional marks whatsoever on the notes prior to placing them in the sealed envelope, and that he then be instructed to deliver this sealed envelope directly to the head of the Belgrade field office as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I would agree with that with one caveat, that I would ask Your Honours to ask from the witness how quickly he could do it with the hope that he could do it within -- immediately upon his return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. He said that would be the first thing he would do upon his return. We'll remind him of that. Second, we have one hour left for cross-examination, Mr. Jordash. One hour minus three minutes because that's -- and I have to read two decisions. I know that the time is short.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think I can finish, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that means approximately 50 minutes. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I can finish in that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break, and we resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I am aware that we lost nine minutes. That was -- there were some reasons for that, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have on the screen, please, P51.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to return to -- Mr. Kovacevic, I want to return to your suggestion that somehow you hadn't said things in your 2003 statement about state security department because you hadn't been informed about the case that you were going to be testifying in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We've got a problem with e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have to log in again, or? If that's it, I had to as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Maybe. Please could we have paragraph 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 38, as you can see, starts off with a discussion about where you were billeted in Eastern Slavonia. And halfway down the paragraph says, it says: "The SAO SBZS formed police units in all the above-mentioned settlements after they were liberated. The MUP of Serbia supplied them with uniform, weapons, and other equipment, and they sewed SAO SBZS insignia onto the uniforms." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you gave evidence during your interview in 2003 about the role that the MUP of Serbia played in supplying the police stations; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And those police stations then went about their work in bringing in looters and dealing with crime in the region; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with our assistance, training, and jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if we look at paragraph 41, the statement says, at the beginning of the paragraph: "Some of our orders concerned police work such as bringing in looters, while other orders had do with combat action. Radovan Stojicic, Badza, commanded our unit."

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then it says: "We received orders for combat action from the JNA, but Stojicic, Badza, had to be informed of these orders and approve them before we were allowed to act upon them." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the command of the JNA of units deployed in the area, to be precise, that was the Novi Sad corps command and the units there, co-ordination was carried out with Radovan Stojicic, Badza, concerning the engaging of our units.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the paragraph reads on that: "Our commander Zarko Sljukic received his orders from Lieutenant-Colonel Vaskovic, from the Ruma Division, and from his deputy Mrda, also a lieutenant-colonel, when we were active in the zone of responsibility." So what you were saying, is this right, Mr. Kovacevic, is that when it came to police station work and the dealing with crime, Badza was in command and giving orders; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He issued commands to our officers, which particular manpower would be used for some civilian affairs; and other men that were engaged in war operations in co-ordination with the JNA was done in agreement with our -- between our command, Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and JNA units deployed in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. So JNA -- the JNA commanders such as Major-General Bratic, commander of the Novi Sad corps, would give orders to your unit concerning combat, and those orders had to be approved by Stojicic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be passed on to the commands of our units.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So Stojicic wasn't in command of the JNA, was he? But the JNA was in command, at times, of your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Radovan Stojicic, Badza, did not have any authority to issue orders to the Yugoslav People's Army; but depending on the situation on the ground and the use of JNA and our units, daily meeting would be held to agree upon certain matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Then reading on to paragraph 42: "We received fuel and other materiel for combat action from the JNA." So is this correct: Because of the lack of sophisticated weapons in the possession of your brigade and in the possession of Badza, whenever your unit went into combat it had to rely upon the JNA weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we had our personal weapons, as I said, rifles and pistols. As for the rest, before we went into action, we received ammunition for automatic rifles and pistols, and we also received hand-grenades and Zoljas.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Let's read on to -- in 42: "The JNA had many problems because it was made up almost entirely of reservists. There were a few regular soldiers, and they were quite disorganised at the beginning. The units of the Serbian MUP, which had arrived there, were better organised." Is that correct? Yes or no will do.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The next paragraph is the one I'm particularly interested in: "They sent our unit, Arkan's Men, or other volunteers wherever there was fierce fighting, such as attacks on fortifications or mopping-up operations." Is that correct, that the JNA sent Arkan's Men wherever there was fierce fighting?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In co-ordination with the Novi Sad corps command, the Territorial Defence, our units, and the units of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, since our units, and particularly the units of the Serbian Volunteer Guard were much better prepared and trained than JNA units for mopping up, our units and Serbian Volunteer Guard Units would be sent on such missions, because initially there was lack of discipline among the ranks of JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So why, when you gave the Prosecution this paragraph in 2003, didn't you say at that point that Arkan's Men were under the command of the DB? You were there giving evidence about Arkan's Men and who commanded them in combat; why didn't you say anything about the DB?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was giving a general statement, and I said that the Serbian Volunteer Guard was there in the area and the rest of it. Nobody asked any question about that, and that's why I never said that the Serbian Volunteer Guard had been formed by the state security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What was Radovan Stojicic's position in the Serbian MUP at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which position he held in 1991. All I know is that he was there in the field, commanding the TO of Eastern Slavonia and West Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, you didn't speak to one of your many sources to find out where he was in the general hierarchy of the Serbian MUP? No one ever mentioned that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one mentioned anything about his status in the MUP of Serbia. I know that upon his return from the area he was promoted, and he later became assistant minister for public order in the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: He was the deputy minister -- he became the deputy minister in, I think, February of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date of his appointment when he became minister. I think it was upon his return from Eastern Slavonia and West Srem. I wasn't privy to the promotions and other appointments in the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Or who reported to who? You weren't privy to that information either, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have exact information about hierarchy; but from conversations and through meetings, I knew that the Serbian Volunteer Guard was under the control of the DB. And sometimes when I drove my officers, I would say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We were talking about Badza. I know you're very keen to say the accused were responsible for the DB, so the accused were responsible for Arkan, but we'll come to that in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The comments are -- should have been left out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go back to the subject, Mr. Kovacevic. You don't know who Badza reported to in 1991? From your own admission, you don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be able to know exactly from whom he received his orders from Belgrade. I can't even say who sent him to the field and who appointed him commander of TO of Eastern Slavonia and West Srem because according to his birth place he wasn't in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you don't know but you told the Prosecution that he was under the direct control of the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, P53.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why would you tell the Prosecution - we can turn to it if you want - why would you tell the Prosecution that Badza was under the direct control of the Serbian DB if you do not know exactly from whom he received his orders from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a conversation with my officers while we were returning from a meeting, one of the officers said that Mr. Radovan Stojicic, Badza, was receiving direct command from the state security service, and that is the reason why I stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So your sole evidence for that conclusion that Badza was under the direct control of the Serbian DB was a single conversation in 1991; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move to Arkan. What's your evidence about Arkan, who he reported to, other than those we discussed in the statement from 2003?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Units of the Serbian Volunteer Guard were not supplied with weapons and ammunition from the JNA as we did. They had their own stockpiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's it? Is that why you say they must have been under control of the DB because they had different -- a different weapons supply?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only because of that. They were considerably better equipped than we were. They even had 9 millimetre Heckler and Koch weapons; some of their officers had 9 millimetre Berettas; they had overalls; they had more sophisticated bulletproof vests; and generally they were better equipped. And the source of that equipment and everything else was not the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But when you -- your unit arrived in Eastern Slavonia under the command of Badza, doesn't it follow from what you've said that your unit and Badza was being supplied by the DB?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We came there with the equipment and uniforms issued to us, and the ammunition and food was replenished by the JNA units deployed in that area. On the other hand, the Serbian Volunteer Guard were organised in such a way that they had their own food and ammunition and equipment provided from a different source.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But did you not then at the time say to anyone, How come we in the police unit under the command of the DB have been supplied weapons which are not even nearly as good as those supplied to Arkan, since the weapons supply on your evidence was the same? Didn't you query that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With our police brigade, as I said, we were issued 7.62 millimetre rifles and 7.60 pistols, all of the Zastava make. Units of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, as far as I know, were not issued with either the equipment or weapons in the state security department of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on after this one question: You don't know, do you, who Arkan, if anyone, reported to aside from those who were in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From conversations with my superior officers and from experience in the field, I learnt that the Serbian Volunteer Guard was responsible to the state security department. As I said, the Serbian Volunteer Guard oversaw traffic at bridge and all, and any goods shipped from Serbia across the bridge into Eastern Slavonia could not obtain passage without their clearance. Even the JNA units and our units, whenever we went on furlough for a day or two back home, we were checked. As we were on our way back home for rest for a day or two, we were not allowed to carry our weapons with us. We had to leave them behind, both rifles and pistols. To carry weapons, we needed to obtain specific authorisation by our superior officers -- or, rather, the only thing we could carry along were pistols.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move on. Who do you say -- no, let me ask a different question. In 2009, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's have, if we can, P53 on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In 2009, Mr. Kovacevic, you decided that Captain Dragan Vasiljevic [sic] was also under the control of the Serbian DB. Paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The word "decided" is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is somewhat aggressive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, when Mr. Kovacevic testified last year, there was not -- a B/C/S translation of this document was not available. There is one now, and it has been uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if you need that, it's there, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, perhaps we can shortcut this. Who did Captain Dragan Vasiljevic [sic] report to in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gentleman who was known at the time only as Captain Dragan - whose last name is "Vasiljkovic" and not "Vasiljevic" - was under the control of the state security service. To the best of my knowledge and based on information I learned subsequently, in the area of Knin where their camp was situated in Golubic it was Mr. Frenki Simatovic who took Captain Dragan to that area and called on him to train units that were subsequently styled Knindzes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When did you learn this, Mr. Kovacevic, the information you learned subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that it was the state security service that engaged him when I was out in the field in 1991. Now, specific information and facts I came to know from an interview that was held on Studio B52 [as interpreted] station where Mr. Vasiljkovic himself said that it was Mr. Frenki Simatovic who invited him to the area of the RSK. He also said that they met in Hotel Metropol on Bulevar Revolucije Street in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we turn, please, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry to interrupt, but this will be important for our Defence. There's a mistake in the transcript which I believe I can correct, and it's that the TV in Belgrade is called "B92," not "B52."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's almost common knowledge, but did you refer to B92, Witness? Is that what you intended to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have, please, P51, paragraph 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Paragraph 53. You, in 2003, said this about Captain Dragan: "I believe it was shortly before the end of October or in early November when Captain Dragan's Knindze's arrived at the Vukovar battle-field via Bosnia. His unit had between 30 and 50 men. They were deployed near the Djergaj forest, and the name of the commander of that unit was Lieutenant Lale. Another part of his group was deployed between Luzac and Borovo Naselje." Do you recall telling the Prosecution that in 2003?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Our unit when to the Brsadiski Lug [phoen], where the observation post of the army was, went often to that particular observation post --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Kovacevic, I don't want to cut you off, but I'm just asking you whether you said that to the Prosecution in 2003. Yes or no? I'm running out of time.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Is there any reason why you didn't say that Captain Dragan was under the control of Frenki Simatovic and the DB when you gave evidence in 2003? When you gave this statement in 2003?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained this earlier. There's no need for me to repeat this. When I was giving my statement in 2003 on two occasions in Belgrade, I recounted the facts as recorded in my notes. The Prosecution did not know in which of the cases my statement would be used, and they didn't go into any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. If that's your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go to paragraph 89, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just want to understand something about what you were doing in 1993 and 1994. Perhaps I can shortcut this. Am I correct that from April of 1994 until December of 1994 you were working for private companies?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you continued working for private companies and you were involved in these -- the transportation of various goods into Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After I returned on the 14th of January, 1994, from my field posting near Gorazde, I spent some time at Kosa 4. Afterwards, once a vehicle was requisitioned from the Borovica company by the MUP and since the company owning the department stores had already gone bankrupt, I joined a private company in Novi Sad for a while and then moved on to the Borovica company owned by Mr. Borovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And they were -- they were giving -- you were receiving instructions from the private companies when you were involved in the transport of these various goods; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name of the company.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The owner, Nedzo Mandic, agreed to place some of his vehicles at the disposal of the Yugoslav Army for their purposes, since there was not much business in international transport at the time anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go to paragraph 97, please. Sorry, 94.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, we now missed the name of the company, but it seems not to be very relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's in the statement, Your Honour. If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Please ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 94 states: "I returned to my firm in early April 1994 and stayed there until December 1994, when I left my firm because it had gone bankrupt." Now, missing out a few lines, the statement then says: "As at that time, Yugoslavia was under sanctions imposed by the international community. There was no work for truck drivers, so that the trucks would get used by the VJ and the Ministry of Defence." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went back to my post in the department store company but decided to move on to the Partnertrans Company in Novi Sad. Their vehicles had been placed at the disposal of the Ministry of Defence and the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it was the Ministry of Defence and the Yugoslav Army who were involved in the transportation of these goods, using their trucks which had been taken from private companies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had their schedule from the Army of Yugoslavia; they were provided with fuel by the Army of Yugoslavia; and they carried out tasks that were given to them by the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it was the Army of Yugoslavia who made the arrangements for transporting the oil to the Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia sent oil to Republika Srpska for their needs, probably based on an agreement between Republika Srpska and Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it was the Yugoslav -- the Army of Yugoslavia who were involved in registering the vehicles as they transported the goods in convoy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it was the Yugoslav Army who ensured that the convoys were safely delivered to the Republika Srpska and the Republika Srpska Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia took care of loading the goods and distributing them. We had the security detail from the Army of Yugoslavia and the MUP of Serbia accompanying us up to the border of Republika Srpska, where we would be met by the security service of Republika Srpska and their police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. The MUP of Serbia - it was the police officers who would accompany, on occasion, the convoys; is that correct, up to the border of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were military vehicles accompanying us. As I said, the convoy would be formed at Motel Srem, on the highway next to Sremska Mitrovica. From there on, members of the MUP of Serbia would provide security. And as we proceeded onto the Zagreb-Belgrade motorway, we would be directed to the lane. We would have one vehicle of the MUP accompanying us on the right-hand side, on the right-hand side lane, making sure that we could make a turn safely; and then there were other vehicles to our left, making sure that we had smooth passage on our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the MUP of Serbia were fellow police officers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, members of the traffic service.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And -- That's all I have. Thank you very much, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, one -- if I might, just one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- issue I think I should put, in fairness to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware, Mr. Kovacevic, that the Banjica location that you described yesterday was, in fact, in 1991, and had been from 1970 until 1992, the federal institute for security under the control of the federal government and the federal MUP, nothing to do with the Serbian DB? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that. Just as the building of the federal SUP on Kneza Milosa is across the MUP of Serbia, and in 1991 or 1992 it was transferred within the competence of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that's -- I can leave it there. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave from Mr. Jordash's cross-examination, there arose an issue which had not been addressed so far. If I can be allowed three to five minutes to address it, I believe it proper to address the issue before Mr. Groome, unless you deem it fit for Mr. Groome to proceed first in his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you first tell it -- tell us what it is, then, so -- before I give you three to five minutes. You know that we are running out of time. It's rather unusual, though not --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know, Your Honour; however, it has been the first time that we heard this from the witness - and I do have his proofing note from 2009, which states something else - and this is that Captain Dragan was taken by Frenki Simatovic to the Krajina in 1991. And I can show you the document we have to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you are allowed to raise this question, but please be efficient and focused.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'll do my best. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Bakrac:

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Witness, let us first make one thing clear: At page 59, lines 10 to 12, you talked about the time when you learned this fact. Let's be quite clear. Back in 1991, did you know that it was Mr. Frenki Simatovic who allegedly took Captain Dragan to the Krajina in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that it was Mr. Frenki Simatovic, specifically, who took Captain Dragan to the SAO Krajina. Rather, from conversations with individuals who came to Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem as members of the Knindzes, I heard that he acted within the purview of state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just add that I learned this fact from his interview that he gave a couple of years back to Studio B92, and I'm sure you can obtain this interview from them if you so wish. Those were his very words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please, I don't have time for this. The fact that it was Frenki who took Captain Dragan there is something that you learned from Studio B92 but when exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember when his interview was broadcast. Was it a year or two ago? What I can state for a fact is that I watched the interview and then I'm sure that B92 possesses that footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not primarily interested in hearing from the witness what he saw on television because then we have perhaps a million people who could tell us what they saw on television, and that's not a source the Chamber would easily rely upon, unless it is, of course, heavily supported with other material.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm precisely about to deal with this. I would only like the witness first to say briefly the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you see the footage before your testimony here in 2009 or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly whether it was before or after.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we call up P53, please. Specifically paragraph 15, which relates to Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: On the 24th or the 25th of August, 2009, this witness, at page 15, stated as follows. Rather than me reading out the whole paragraph, let's took at the context: Captain Dragan Vasiljkovic was under the control of the state security service in Serbia. He had been recommended by a late member of the DB, Klara Mandic, and Dafina Milanovic financed Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the information I had in 1991 in the field in Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem. This information dates back to that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why on the -- when on the 25th of August Klause Hoffmann asked you about this, did you say that it was Frenki Simatovic who took Captain Dragan to Knin -- rather, why didn't you tell him that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because I didn't have that information. I don't recall whether it was before my testimony that I saw the B92 broadcast or afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I don't have any more questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Groome, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, with respect to your criminal history, do you currently have any pending cases?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you have anything to gain by knowingly testifying falsely in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only stating the facts that I knew and that I was aware of. I don't have any reasons to accuse anyone of anything. Nobody did anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I have a few questions with respect to your notes. Did you personally draft the notes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was your practice? How long after an event would you record it in your notes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it all depended on the situation. If something happened, I would make a note of it right away or else I would do it when I had a moment to spare. I recorded the time, the people concerned, and the events that transpired.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. You say you recorded the time. Did you also record the date on which the events occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The notes, are they individual pieces of paper or is it a bound book or bound books?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was written on A4 sheets of paper that I subsequently stapled and bound in a plastic cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Over the course of the intervening years, have any portion of your notes been misplaced, damaged, lost, or stolen?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is there anything unique about these notes themselves that will make it clear to us that when we eventually receive them that they are, in fact, the very notes that you have given evidence about yesterday and today? Is there anything strikingly unique, perhaps on the first page or anywhere on the notes?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is only written there that it's my journal and that you can see that I started writing it in 1991 when I was out in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. The re-examination has not triggered any need for further questions. Then this concludes your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, this concludes your testimony. You told us that you would be willing to give your notes to the Tribunal. Would you please listen very carefully to the instructions I'm going to give and which relate to you. First, we'll ask the Victims and Witness Section to give to you, Mr. Kovacevic, a large, sealable envelope with the address of this Chamber on it, noting the name of this case and also your name, Mr. Kovacevic. Mr. Kovacevic, what we want you to do and what you're instructed to do is the following: You place your notes in that envelope and you seal the envelope. You should not review. So don't go through the notes again, don't review them, don't make any corrections of any kind to the notes, and do not add anything to the notes prior to placing them in the sealed envelope. And then you should deliver this sealed envelope directly to the head of the Belgrade field office as soon as possible. Could you tell us how much time you think you would need to deliver it at the Belgrade field office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This envelope, as well as a photocopy of my military booklet, would be -- will be in the Belgrade field office on Monday next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could the instructions be conveyed to the Victims and Witness Section. They may follow the proceedings so that we -- that everyone is knowing what is expected from him or her. Mr. Kovacevic, I'd like to thank you for coming, not only once but even twice, to The Hague and to testify. And you have answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench; I thank you for that. And I'd like to wish you a safe return home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I really, out of respect for this Court, made an effort to come two days after my surgery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 6th day of September, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
